findings.title: BaseCalendarService.createEvent does not match new Calendar interface signature
findings.body: The Calendar interface in packages/types/Calendar.d.ts now requires `createEvent(event, credentialId)`, but this class still implements `async createEvent(event: CalendarEvent)` with no `credentialId` parameter. This is a TypeScript contract violation for any app that extends BaseCalendarService (e.g. caldav-style providers), and at runtime this implementation does not filter `event.destinationCalendar` by credential, so on a collective event whose first entry is a Google/Lark calendar it will request the wrong external id and likely fail.

findings.title: Google updateEvent lookup compares externalId against externalCalendarId (broken)
findings.body: `const selectedCalendar = externalCalendarId ? externalCalendarId : event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId;` When `externalCalendarId` is falsy we then run `.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)`, i.e. search for an entry whose `externalId === undefined`. That never matches, so `selectedCalendar` is `undefined` and is passed straight to `calendar.events.update` as `calendarId`. The delete branch on line 315-317 has the same bug but without the `"primary"` fallback that the create branch uses, so deletion on the Google API will fail.

findings.title: Google deleteEvent lookup always yields undefined
findings.body: `const calendarId = externalCalendarId ? externalCalendarId : event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId;` The `.find` predicate requires `cal.externalId === externalCalendarId`; since we are in the falsy branch of the ternary this becomes `cal.externalId === undefined`, never true. Result: an undefined `calendarId` is sent to `calendar.events.delete`, breaking deletions whenever a booking does not have a stored externalCalendarId.

findings.title: updateEvent return is missing externalId/credentialId, breaking editLocation references
findings.body: `EventResult` now declares `externalId?: string | null` and the `updateLocation` flow in EventManager.ts (lines ~200-211) reads `result.externalId` and `result.credentialId` to build `referencesToCreate`. But `CalendarManager.updateEvent` still returns only `{appName, type, success, uid, updatedEvent, originalEvent, calError, calWarnings}` without those two fields. As a result, every references row created by `updateLocation` will have `externalCalendarId: undefined`, losing the link to the underlying calendar event used by `deleteEvent`.

findings.title: Lark createEvent always uses the first destination calendar regardless of credential
findings.body: EventManager.create iterates over each destination and calls `createEvent(credential, event, destination.externalId)` to drive the per-host booking. Lark's createEvent ignores the credential/externalId it was given and falls back to `event.destinationCalendar ?? []` (first element). In a collective event whose first destination belongs to a Google host, Lark will be asked to create the event under that Google external id and the request will fail or write to the wrong calendar.

findings.title: Office365 createEvent ignores credentialId and may address the wrong calendar
findings.body: Same pattern as Lark: the new Calendar interface and EventManager pass `credentialId` and `destination.externalId`, but Office365's implementation just takes `event.destinationCalendar[0]`. For a collective event the first destination is typically the main host's calendar (e.g. Google), so the Office365 call would attempt `https://graph.microsoft.com/.../calendars/<google-external-id>/events` and fail.

findings.title: teamDestinationCalendars pushed without dedup; can create duplicate events on same calendar
findings.body: `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars);` has no de-duplication by `credentialId`/`externalId`. Hosts that share a single connected destination calendar (a common case when multiple members point at the same Google account) will each contribute the same entry, leading EventManager.create to call `createEvent` twice for the same calendar+credential and create duplicate events in that calendar.

findings.title: Cancellation only includes a single destination calendar, losing team calendars
findings.body: The CalendarEvent built here wraps only `bookingToDelete.destinationCalendar` or the user destination in a single-element array and never collects other team hosts' destinations. handleNewBooking now aggregates host destination calendars into a multi-element array for new bookings; cancellation must do the same or cancellations on collective events will leak the secondary calendars (their events still exist because `deleteEvent` is called per reference, but emails/webhooks reflect only one calendar and the symmetry between create and cancel is broken).

findings.title: destinationCalendar built without user.destinationCalendar fallback, inconsistent with other handlers
findings.body: All sibling handlers (confirm, cancelBooking, editLocation, handleNewBooking, deleteCredential, paypal/stripe webhooks, bookingReminder) fall back to `user.destinationCalendar` when `booking.destinationCalendar` is null. This handler does not, so for users whose only destinationCalendar lives on the user (not the booking), the request-reschedule flow will silently go through with `destinationCalendar: []`, which EventManager.create interprets as 'no destination'.

findings.title: When merging bookings, only first calendar reference of the old booking is deleted
findings.body: `const oldCalendarEvent = booking.references.find((reference) => reference.type.includes("_calendar"));` returns at most one reference. For a collective reschedule that produced multiple calendar references on the old booking, only the first one will be deleted on its provider. The remaining calendar events stay on the user's calendar and effectively become orphans.

findings.title: loadUsers try/catch swallows programming errors and converts them to 500/400
findings.body: The new wrapping of `loadUsers` in a try/catch that maps `Prisma.PrismaClientKnownRequestError` to statusCode 400 and any other error to statusCode 500 masks real bugs (e.g. wrong select shape, missing relations). Also the `if (!Array.isArray(hosts)) throw` is unreachable: `hosts` was already set via `eventType.hosts || []`, so it is always an array. These added checks give a false sense of guarding a code path that cannot fail as written.

findings.title: Main-host external id reused as organizer email even when event is created on another host's calendar
findings.body: `email: mainHostDestinationCalendar?.externalId ? mainHostDestinationCalendar.externalId : calEventRaw.organizer.email,` is taken from the FIRST destination calendar (the main host's calendar), but the actual insertion below happens on the calendar returned by `destinationCalendar?.find(c => c.credentialId === credentialId)`, which may be a different host. As a result, when a non-main host's Google calendar is the target, the organizer entry in that calendar's event will be the main host's externalId/email instead of the true calendar owner's.

findings.title: PR makes no new tests for the multi-host collective booking flow it claims to fix
findings.body: The change converts `destinationCalendar` from a single object to an array and rewires creation/cancellation across many files, fixing #7754 (collective events with multiple destination calendars per host). The PR description itself notes 'I haven't added tests that prove my fix is effective'. The existing `webhook.e2e.ts` update only changes the expected `destinationCalendar` literal in a single webhook assertion, which does not exercise the new per-host creation or per-host cancellation flow.
